name: tsl::array_map / array-hash (Tessil)
workload: String-keyed map (key to 32-bit int): insert all keys, then look up all keys. Wikipedia enwiki-20170320 ns0 titles (13,099,148 keys, avg length 19.90, shuffled) and Askitis distinct_1 insert / skew1_1 read (28,772,169 / 177,999,203 keys, avg length 9.59 / 5.06); memory measured too. All hash maps use CityHash64.
claimed_speedup: Wikipedia shuffled: read 138.24 ns/key vs 173.58 for std::unordered_map (1.26x faster, derived from page data); memory 678.73 MiB vs 1246.60 MiB (1.84x less, derived from page data); insert with reserve 249.52 vs 350.33 ns/key (1.40x faster, derived from page data); insert without reserve 603.94 vs 590.88 ns/key (about equal, 2% slower). Askitis dataset: read 46.41 vs 105.05 ns/key (2.26x faster, derived from page data); insert with reserve 244.19 vs 309.06 ns/key (1.27x faster, derived from page data); insert without reserve 545.82 vs 554.02 ns/key (about equal); memory 1031.67 vs 2110.19 MiB (2.05x less, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 6.3 on Debian Stretch x64 (README); benchmark Makefile in the linked gist: CXXFLAGS=-lcityhash -std=c++11 -march=native -DNDEBUG -O3
hardware: Intel i5-5200u, 8 GB RAM; best of 20 runs (hat-trie README)
tradeoffs: Header-only, C++11. Stores keys as packed char arrays instead of std::string, so there is no std::pair<const Key,T> and no stable references: any modifying operation invalidates iterators, references and pointers. Rehash is slow and needs spare memory because keys are copied (cannot be moved). Default max key size 65,535 and max 2^32 elements (template parameters). Erase may delay value destruction. Default hash is std::hash<std::string_view> or FNV-1a, so a faster hash (CityHash gives about 40% faster reads per the README) must be supplied by the user. Bucket-level API is missing.
caveats: The numbers are on the hat-trie README page (the array-hash README only links to the author's blog benchmark, tessil.github.io, which is egress-blocked here and was not read). Benchmark dates from 2017: GCC 6.3, a dual-core ultrabook CPU, and the comparison set is std::unordered_map, tsl::hopscotch_map, google::dense_hash_map, spp::sparse_hash_map and the tries; absl::flat_hash_map and tsl::robin_map are not in the table, so the listed absl and robin baselines are not covered. Baseline stdlib is libstdc++ by inference (GCC on Debian), not stated outright. std::unordered_map is keyed on std::string (32 bytes minimum per key), which handicaps it on memory by design. Insert is not faster without reserve (about equal on both datasets), and lookups are slower than tsl::hopscotch_map (138.24 vs 119.49 ns/key on Wikipedia) and about equal on Askitis; dense_hash_map reads slightly faster on Askitis (43.09 ns). The README says best of 20 runs, but the gist's Makefile invokes each binary once per run, so the 20-run driver is not in the gist. Peak memory with array_map without reserve (823.54 MiB) is higher than final memory because of rehash copies. Flags were read through a WebFetch summary of the gist (twice, consistent), not a raw download (gist.githubusercontent.com is blocked).

name: DeLZSA (ivagorRetrocomp)
workload: No benchmark found: decompressing LZSA1/LZSA2 streams on Intel 8080 and PDP-11 processors.
stars_or_usage: Listed under 'External links' in the emmanuel-marty/lzsa README (261 stars) as 'i8080 and PDP-11 decompressors by Ivan Gorodetsky'
tradeoffs: Targets 8-bit and 16-bit retro CPUs (Intel 8080, PDP-11), not modern machines. Decompresses the LZSA formats only (LZSA1 designed to replace LZ4, LZSA2 to replace ZX7 on 8-bit systems).
caveats: The repo could not be opened on 2026-10-07: WebFetch of the repo page, its /tree/main page and the owner page returned HTTP 404, and raw.githubusercontent.com README.md and readme.md on main and master returned 404 (the repo may be deleted, renamed or private). Its existence and description come only from the LZSA README (opened) and two WebSearch snippets. No README, license, speed table or size table was seen, so tier D, license unknown (usability reference), has_code set false because no code was reachable, last commit unknown. A DeLZSA decompressor is not an alternative to the LZSA reference decompressor in the usual sense: the reference decompressor is a C program for modern machines, while DeLZSA ports the format to 8080 and PDP-11 assembly, so a throughput win over the baseline is not even a well-defined comparison. The only speed figures near this topic are from the LZSA README (LZSA1 decompression about 90% of LZ4 speed, LZSA2 about 75%, on 8-bit systems), which concern the format, not DeLZSA. Not notable by stars; kept as the orchestrator's seed record only.

name: bzip2gpu (weissenberger)
baseline: multicore CPU bzip2 decompressor (exact program not named in the search snippet; candidates bzip2, pbzip2, lbzip2)
workload: bzip2 decompression on a GPU: Huffman decoding, RLE2, inverse MTF, inverse BWT and RLE1 all on the device, output kept in device memory (README). The paper (ICPP 2024, 'Massively Parallel Inverse Block-sorting Transforms for bzip2 Decompression on GPUs', DOI 10.1145/3673038.3673067 per the README) evaluates on an A100 GPU and a DGX H100 server.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only: up to 6.1x over a multicore CPU implementation for the inverse BWT stage; up to 2400 MB/s combined inverse BWT and inverse MTF on an A100; over 11.62 GB/s bzip2 archive decompression on a DGX H100. The README itself states no numbers. No whole-archive CPU baseline figure was seen.
compiler_and_flags: Makefile (opened): nvcc -std=c++17 -O3 -arch=native -Xcompiler "-Wall -std=c++17 -O3 -march=native -fopenmp"; README requires GNU compiler 11.4.1+ and CUDA SDK 12.4.1+. Flags used for the paper's numbers are not seen.
hardware: Per the paper snippet: NVIDIA A100 and a DGX H100 server; CPU model for the baseline not seen. README: CUDA GPU with compute capability 7.0 or higher.
tradeoffs: Needs a CUDA GPU (compute capability 7.0+), proprietary drivers and GNU/Linux. Streams limited to 2^31 - 1 uncompressed bytes (no batching yet). The parser still runs on the CPU. Output stays in device memory, so throughput numbers exclude the copy back to host. Decompress only; no compressor. src/rle.cu and include/thrust_custom_alloc.cuh contain modified Thrust code under Apache-2.0 with LLVM exceptions (also OSI-approved); the rest is MIT.
caveats: The paper is behind blocked hosts (doi.org, dl.acm.org and researchgate returned EGRESS_BLOCKED; no mirror found in the repo or in github.com/weissenberger or github.com/JGU-HPC). The numbers above come from a WebSearch result snippet summarising the abstract, so per the cloud-harness rule the tier is capped at C even though the paper is peer-reviewed; a verifier who can open the paper should retier (likely B or A if the artifact is public) and fix the baseline name. The snippet's 6.1x is for one stage (iBWT) against an unnamed multicore CPU implementation, and the 11.62 GB/s figure carries no baseline in the snippet, so the claim of beating bzip2, pbzip2 or lbzip2 on whole-archive decompression is not confirmed. Repo is explicitly 'auxiliary material for our publication and is not suitable for production use'. The README TODO list includes 'stream error detection (parsing, checksums,...)': in src/parser.cc the block CRC32 is parsed into block_checksums (line 243) but main.cc, bz2gpu.cc and parser.cc never verify it (the .cu files were not read), so corrupt streams are not detected. Only 2 commits (2024-07-15, 2024-07-16), no unit tests (TODO), no benchmark scripts or datasets in the repo (only test/lichess_puzzles_10M.bz2, 10 MB).
